title: Photon anti-bunching in high harmonic generation
authors: Philipp Stammer, Javier Rivera-Dean, Maciej Lewenstein
abstract: Photon anti-bunching is the direct evidence for the existence of photons without having a classical counterpart. Unlike bunching of photons, which can have a semi-classical description, the effect of photon anti-bunching can only be understood with quantized electromagnetic fields. However, for the process of high harmonic generation (HHG), where many photons of the driving field are upconverted to a single photon of higher energy, there is yet no clear evidence for the presence of individual photon emission. The key result of this work is the prediction of photon anti-bunching in the process of HHG, marking it the first theoretical discovery of non-classicality in the temporal correlations of HHG photons. While other non-classical signatures in HHG, such as sub-Poissonian statistics or squeezing, have been discussed for an ensemble of photons, the anti-bunching signature reported here is a signature of a single photon. This is achieved by using the recently developed Heisenberg picture approach for quantum optical HHG, revealing clear anti-bunching signatures in the intensity correlation function across the entire harmonic spectrum.
summary: This paper theoretically predicts photon anti-bunching in High Harmonic Generation (HHG), providing the first evidence of single-photon temporal correlations in this process. Using advanced quantum field techniques, the authors calculate the intensity correlation function $g^{(2)}(	au)$, demonstrating that the emission violates classical bounds when considering only one emitted photon. This work is crucial for understanding non-classical light sources generated in intense laser fields.
main_problem: The primary goal is to theoretically predict and demonstrate photon anti-bunching—a signature of single-photon emission—within the complex process of High Harmonic Generation (HHG). This marks a first theoretical discovery of non-classical temporal correlations in HHG.
main_result: The authors successfully predicted clear evidence of photon anti-bunching ($g^{(2)}(0) < 1$) across the entire harmonic spectrum using quantum field theory methods. They also distinguished this single-photon signature from ensemble statistics like sub-Poissonian distributions.
method: The analysis relies on calculating high-order time correlation functions, specifically $G^{(2)}(	au)$, derived from the Heisenberg picture approach applied to the dipole moment operators within the HHG process.
model_or_system: The system is High Harmonic Generation (HHG), modeled quantum mechanically using a Hamiltonian incorporating field and interaction terms. The analysis progresses from single-atom calculations to many-emitter scenarios, treating the emission as an upconversion of multiple driving photons into one high-energy harmonic photon.
key_observables: Normalized second-order intensity correlation function ($g^{(2)}(	au)$) and the Mandel Q-parameter ($Q$).
important_parameters: Harmonic order ($q$), time delay ($	au$), and the number of emitters ($N$).
main_assumptions: The calculations assume an initial vacuum state for the field and utilize approximations that allow separating correlations into coherent and incoherent parts, especially in the many-emitter limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $g^{(2)}(	au)$ violating classical bounds (showing anti-bunching) for various harmonics and show how this correlation function approaches unity as the number of emitters ($N$) increases.
paper_structure: The paper develops from establishing the theoretical framework using quantum field operators in the Heisenberg picture, calculating $g^{(2)}(	au)$ for single atoms to confirm anti-bunching, and finally extending the analysis to many emitters while distinguishing between temporal correlations (anti-bunching) and number statistics (sub-Poissonian).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it provides a rigorous theoretical pathway to observe fundamental non-classical light sources using an established, high-intensity physical process like HHG.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematics of an experimental HBT-configuration to measure the second-order field correlation function, g(2)(τ), by means of the intensity correlations between the detectors at time I(t) and I(t + τ). While the equal time correlation func- tion g(2)(0) allows to infer on the photon number distribution, only the temporal correlation as a function of τ can conclude on photon anti-bunching via g(2)(0) < g(2)(τ).

FIG. 2. We show the normalized second-order correlation function g(2)(τ) for the relevant range of non-perturbative odd har- monics in the plateau (a) q ∈{11, 13, 15} and (b) q ∈{17, 19}, while in (c) q ∈{21, 23} near the cut-off (for the low-order harmonics we refer to the Appendix B in which the same behavior is shown). The time-delay τ is taken to be after one complete cycle of the driving laser field T = 2π/ω, and evaluated at K = 50 delay times. The driving field parameters are E0 = 0.053 a.u. ωL = 0.057 a.u., and Ip = 0.5 a.u., corresponding to that of hydrogen (see SM for details).

FIG. 4. Mandel Q-parameter as a function of the harmonic or- ders indicating sub-Poissonian photon statistics as Q < 0. The Q-parameter is shown for increasing number of emitters N in- cluding log10 N ∈{2.0, 2.7, 3.4, 4.1, 4.8, 5.5, 6.7, 7.0}, where the guiding line indicates a fixed emitter number, and the colors are those from Fig. 2 for the respective harmonic order. The same field conditions as those in Fig. 2 are used.

FIG. 3. Normalized intensity correlation g(2)(τ) of the q = 13 harmonic order for varying number of emitters N (harmonics q = 19 and q = 23 are shown in Fig. 6 of the Appendix B). The atom number increases for increasing color brightness includ- ing log10 N ∈{2.0, 2.7, 3.4, 4.1, 4.8, 5.5, 6.7, 7.0}. The same field conditions as those in Fig. 2 are considered.

The atom number increases for increasing color brightness includ- ing log10 N ∈{2.0, 2.7, 3.4, 4.1, 4.8, 5.5, 6.7, 7.0}. The same field conditions as those in Fig. 2 are used.
